intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome (CLPED1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NECTIN1 gene (600644), also known as PVRL1, on chromosome 11q23.3. Heterozygosity for a NECTIN1 mutation has been associated with sporadic nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate (OFC7) in northern Venezuela.

checks.claim: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome (CLPED1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the NECTIN1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity for a nonsense mutation of PVRL1, W185X, results in an autosomal recessive CL/P syndrome on Margarita Island, CLPED1 (ref. 1).
checks.explanation: The abstract says homozygosity for the PVRL1 (NECTIN1) mutation causes CLPED1. NECTIN1 is the current approved symbol for PVRL1.

checks.claim: NECTIN1 is also known as PVRL1.
checks.evidence_quote: which we identify as PVRL1, encoding nectin-1
checks.explanation: PVRL1 encodes nectin-1. NECTIN1 is the approved symbol, so this restates the paper's gene name.

checks.claim: The NECTIN1 gene is located on chromosome 11q23.3.
checks.evidence_quote: which we identify as PVRL1, encoding nectin-1
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give a chromosomal location. Under the instructions, standard nomenclature such as chromosomal location counts as supported.

checks.claim: Heterozygosity for a NECTIN1 mutation has been associated with sporadic nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate (OFC7) in northern Venezuela.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we demonstrate highly significant association between heterozygosity for this mutation and sporadic, non-syndromic CL/P in northern Venezuela.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this association directly. The OFC7 label is OMIM's own name for the condition.

paragraphs.text: Bustos et al. (1991) described 27 individuals from 7 families on Margarita Island in northeastern Venezuela (Nueva Esparta State). The families were probably related to each other. Affected individuals had ectodermal dysplasia and other anomalies, with variable expressivity, and females were affected as severely as males. All parents were normal. The authors stated that the clinical picture shared by all patients did not fit any of the known ectodermal dysplasias and that previously published cases did not resemble their patients.

He had hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with sparse, brittle, fine, dry hair and hypodontia, a distinctive facial appearance with cleft lip/palate, cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers, and mild mental retardation. Scanning electron microscopy of the hair showed pili torti and pili trianguli et canaliculi.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora et al. (1987) concluded that the syndrome they observed in 2 sibs was most probably inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder. Rodini and Richieri-Costa (1990) described 3 affected brothers born to normal consanguineous parents and called the disorder autosomal recessive. Bustos et al. (1991) concluded that the Margarita Island condition was an autosomal recessive syndrome because all parents were normal, females were affected as severely as males, and the families came from an isolated, inbred population. Suzuki et al. (2000) found that CLPED1 was autosomal recessive. In the Japanese patient reported by Yoshida et al. (2015), who was born of a consanguineous marriage, the mutation was homozygous and both parents were heterozygous for it.

paragraphs.text: Using an affected-only DNA-pooling strategy, Suzuki et al. (1998) mapped the gene for Margarita Island ectodermal dysplasia (ED4) to 11q23 by linkage disequilibrium mapping. Haplotype analysis of 4 complex Margarita Island families placed the gene in an interval of about 1 to 2 Mb spanned by just 2 YACs.

paragraphs.text: By positional cloning, Suzuki et al. (2000) identified PVRL1 (NECTIN1), which encodes nectin-1, as the gene responsible for autosomal recessive CLPED1. Nectin-1 is an immunoglobulin-related transmembrane cell-cell adhesion molecule that is part of the NAP cell adhesion system. It is also the principal cell surface receptor for alpha-herpesviruses (HveC).

paragraphs.text: In a 7-year-old Japanese boy with CLPED1, born of a consanguineous marriage, Yoshida et al. (2015) analyzed exon 2 of the PVRL1 gene and found a homozygous nonsense mutation, c.400C-T (R134X). Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The authors noted that all 4 PVRL1 mutations identified in this syndrome up to that time, including theirs, resulted in truncated proteins. These proteins lack the transmembrane and intracellular domains of nectin-1, which are needed to start the cell-cell adhesion process.
